en: Land heats faster than the ocean during the day, causing warm air to rise and cooler ocean air to rush inland as a sea breeze.
Earthworms consume decaying plant matter and excrete nutrient-rich castings, which naturally fertilize the soil and create tunnels that improve water drainage.
Intense subterranean heat and immense tectonic pressure physically transform soft sedimentary limestone into the hard, crystalline metamorphic rock known as marble.
Plant roots absorb groundwater, which travels up the stem and evaporates into the atmosphere through tiny leaf pores called stomata during transpiration.
Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to receive varying angles of direct sunlight throughout the year, creating the seasons.
Extreme gravitational pressure in a star's core forces hydrogen atoms to fuse together, releasing the massive amounts of light and heat energy we see.
The Moon's gravitational pull creates a tidal bulge in Earth's oceans, causing water levels to rise and fall as our planet rotates.
Tectonic plates slowly slide past each other until friction locks them, building stress that eventually snaps and releases energy as seismic earthquake waves.
Moist ocean air forced upward by mountains like Mt. Pulag cools rapidly and condenses, causing heavy orographic rainfall on the windward slopes.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone bedrock over thousands of years, chemically weathering the rock to carve out massive underground cave systems like Puerto Princesa.
Rainwater slowly seeps through porous soil and cracked rocks, gravity pulling it down to replenish underground aquifers that supply water to local wells.
Thick layers of sand and mud accumulate in river deltas, where heavy burial compacts and cements the particles into solid sedimentary sandstone.
